newsitem.title: UK: Expiring November coffee hogs limelight.
newsitem.headline: Expiring November coffee hogs limelight.

text.p: Coffee stole the limelight among soft commodity options ahead of next week's November expiry with cocoa largely neglected, traders said on Thursday.
Coffee saw 1,122 lots changing hands on Friday, led by March calls at a strike price of $1,400, and traders said there were further enquiries on March.
But activity slowed towards the end of the week as players gathered in London for Britain's annual Coffee Week.
Market attention continued to centre on expiring November $1,600 calls where there is still a large open interest of 1,650 lots, believed by some traders to be controlled by one substantial holder.
"It will be quite interesting to watch next week," said one trader. Two possible scenarios have been offered for likely developments.
"One, it will expire around or under $1,500 if the origins keep on selling. Another scenario is that it may run up to between $1,550 and $1,600 and trigger delta hedging," one said.
"But I kind of favour the first one," he added. "We could see some holders liquidating their positions early next week ahead of expiry."
Coffee futures rallied strongly on Wednesday on arbitrage buying and trade short-covering but the run-up proved shortlived and prices eased back on Thursday.
The November premium to January narrowed slightly this week but remained at around $60 a tonne, reflecting a lack of nearby coffee to fill a supply gap between seasons.
Call volatilities on November options were unchanged at around 28 to 29 percent and remained under selling pressure.
"You will be lucky if you could sell at 30 percent," one broker said.
In cocoa, activity was virtually at a standstill.
"There is not a lot happening in the futures. So people are not interested in options," said one market maker.
Only a very thin volume of March 1,000 stg calls were traded this week.
Strong European grind figures helped cocoa futures to crawl back to the top of their recent range but the optimism was not reflected in the options market.
Traders said it was difficult to judge the level of implied volatilities because of the lack of deals, although March calls were quoted at between 20 and 21 percent last week.
Traders recommended selling the March strangle as a good strategy. This involves selling the 950 stg put and the 1,100 stg call simultaneously.
